questions.question_text: Differentiate $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 6}{\sqrt{x + 2}}$ using the quotient rule, and state any zeros of the derivative function.

options.why: Reversed the quotient-rule numerator to $uv' - u'v$, changing the sign of the derivative.

options.text: $f'(x) = \dfrac{3x + 10}{2(x + 2)\sqrt{x + 2}}$; there are no derivative zeros in the domain.
options.why: Added $u'v$ and $uv'$ instead of subtracting, giving the numerator $2(x + 2) + (x + 6) = 3x + 10$; its zero $x = -10/3$ is outside the domain.
Omitted the $uv'$ term, leaving only $u'v/v^{2} = 1/\sqrt{x + 2}$.

questions.solution_text:
$u = x + 6, \quad u' = 1$
$v = \sqrt{x + 2}, \quad v' = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x + 2}}$
$f'(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 2} - \dfrac{x + 6}{2\sqrt{x + 2}}}{x + 2}$
$= \dfrac{2(x + 2) - (x + 6)}{2(x + 2)\sqrt{x + 2}}$
$= \dfrac{x - 2}{2(x + 2)\sqrt{x + 2}}$
Setting $f'(x) = 0$ gives $x - 2 = 0$, so $x = 2$.
This is in the domain $x > -2$, so the derivative zero is $x = 2$.

questions.question_text: Differentiate $f(x) = \dfrac{2\sqrt{x}}{x + 6}$ using the quotient rule for $x > 0$, and state any zeros of the derivative function.

options.why: Omitted the factor $1/2$ when differentiating $\sqrt{x}$, using $u' = 2/\sqrt{x}$ and obtaining the numerator $2(x + 6) - 2x = 12$.
Dropped the coefficient $2$ when differentiating the numerator, using $u' = 1/(2\sqrt{x})$ and obtaining the numerator $(x + 6) - 4x = 6 - 3x$.

options.text: $f'(x) = \dfrac{3x + 6}{\sqrt{x}(x + 6)^{2}}$; there are no derivative zeros for $x > 0$.
options.why: Added $u'v$ and $uv'$ instead of subtracting, giving the numerator $(x + 6) + 2x = 3x + 6$, whose zero $x = -2$ is outside $x > 0$.

questions.solution_text:
$u = 2\sqrt{x}, \quad u' = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$
$v = x + 6, \quad v' = 1$
$f'(x) = \dfrac{\dfrac{x + 6}{\sqrt{x}} - 2\sqrt{x}}{(x + 6)^{2}}$
$= \dfrac{x + 6 - 2x}{\sqrt{x}(x + 6)^{2}}$
$= \dfrac{6 - x}{\sqrt{x}(x + 6)^{2}}$
Setting $f'(x) = 0$ gives $6 - x = 0$, so $x = 6$.
Since $6 > 0$, the derivative zero is $x = 6$.

questions.question_text: Find a correct form of $f'(x)$ if $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+4}{x-2}$.

options.why: Adds $u'v$ and $uv'$ instead of subtracting, giving $2x(x-2)+(x^2+4)=3x^2-4x+4$.
Reverses the quotient-rule numerator to $uv'-u'v$, giving $(x^2+4)-2x(x-2)=-x^2+4x+4$.
Omits the denominator $(x-2)^2$ required by the quotient rule.

questions.solution_text: Let $u=x^2+4$ and $v=x-2$. Then $u'=2x$ and $v'=1$. The quotient rule gives $f'(x)=\frac{2x(x-2)-(x^2+4)}{(x-2)^2}=\frac{x^2-4x-4}{(x-2)^2}$.
